segments.name: Mestarne, the Village in the Suda

stops.name: Tarsus, the province that carries his name
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction as to the year, attested as to the region. Suda pi 3159 opens 'Pylades, a Cilician, from the village of Mestarne', and the victory inscription CIL VI 10115 = ILS 5197 independently lists a Pylades of Cilicia among defeated pantomimes. No ancient source gives a birth year; the first century BCE is a modern inference from the Augustan floruit, and the date here orders the segment only. Tarsus is the atlas marker for the region and is not a claim about the birthplace.
stops.campa: Cilicia lies along the south coast of Asia Minor, mountains at its back, grain and timber and linen going out through its ports toward Antioch and Alexandria. Somewhere in it a boy is born who will become the most watched body in the capital. The Byzantine lexicon that preserves the fact calls him a Cilician; a stone cut for a rival's victories calls him Pylades of Cilicia. Two sources, centuries apart, agree on the province and on nothing else about his beginning.
suggested_refs: Suda pi 3159, the only ancient statement of his origin
CIL VI 10115 = ILS 5197, the Theoros victory inscription
sources: Suda pi 3159, Suda On Line, cs.uky.edu/~raphael/sol
Theatrum lexicon (theatrum.de/2670), for the Theoros inscription

stops.name: Tarsus, the village of Mestarne
stops.date_confidence: Attested and unlocatable. Suda pi 3159 names the village as Mestarne, kome Mestarnon in the genitive plural, the single most specific detail any source gives about his origin. The place has not been identified on the ground and appears nowhere else in Greek or Latin. Earlier working notes for this file transliterated it Mastarnai; the manuscript form is Mestarnon and is corrected here. Date arbitrary.
stops.campa: The Suda gives a village. Mestarne, in the genitive plural, four syllables that occur in no other Greek or Latin text and that no survey, itinerary or inscription has fixed to ground. It is the most precise thing anybody records about him and it is precise about a place nobody can find. A compiler working nine hundred years after the fact keeps the one detail that would locate a man, and passes the word on without comment. Modern editors print it as the manuscripts have it, Mestarnon, and add no note about where it stood.
suggested_refs: The unlocated Cilician village of Mestarne
sources: Suda pi 3159, Suda On Line, cs.uky.edu/~raphael/sol
No independent attestation of the toponym found; recorded as a gap

stops.name: Tarsus, a name out of the tragedies
stops.date_confidence: Interpretive. Pylades is the name of Orestes's companion in Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides, and imperial pantomimes are repeatedly found bearing mythological names. No ancient source states whether the dancer's was a birth name or a professional one, and no ancient writer remarks on the practice at all; the pattern in the names is a modern observation. Date arbitrary and orders the segment.
stops.campa: In the plays he will spend his life dancing, Pylades is the silent one. He stands at Orestes's shoulder the length of the Choephoroi and speaks once, three lines, and the three lines turn the play. The dancer carries that name into a Roman theatre and never speaks on stage at all. Whether his parents gave it to him in Cilicia or he took it when he began to work, nothing says. Bathyllus, Hylas, Paris: the men he will work among and against carry the same kind of borrowed name.
suggested_refs: The convention of mythological stage names among imperial pantomimes
Aeschylus, Choephoroi 900-902, the three lines of the silent companion
sources: Hall and Wyles, eds., New Directions in Ancient Pantomime (Oxford, 2008), cited at second hand

stops.name: Rome, arrival by a road nobody recorded
stops.date_confidence: Gap, stated as one. No ancient source records when Pylades came to Rome, by what route, in whose company, or in what legal condition, and none names a teacher, a school or an itinerary. Whether he crossed as a slave, a freedman or a free professional is unattested. Date arbitrary and marks only that the crossing precedes the first datable notice. Canonical Rome pin, inherited byte-identical from virgil.journey.json.
stops.campa: Between the village and the city there is nothing. No ship, no year, no owner, no port of entry, no name of a teacher, no first engagement. He arrives already able to do the thing he becomes famous for, which is to carry a whole myth through a masked body while somebody else holds the words. The record's first datable statement about him is not an arrival or a debut but a reform of the art. By the time Rome writes him down he has already changed how the thing is done.
suggested_refs: The absent itinerary between Cilicia and Rome
sources: Assessed as a gap across Suetonius, Cassius Dio, Athenaeus, Macrobius, Jerome and the Suda

stops.name: Rome, Campus Martius: what the instrument is
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction, describing the art rather than a dated event; the date orders the segment. The technical account of imperial pantomime, a masked solo dancer taking every role, a sung libretto, pipes and the beaten scabellum, rests on modern scholarship, chiefly E. J. Jory and the essays in Hall and Wyles, eds., New Directions in Ancient Pantomime, not consulted directly this session. The Campus Martius pin marks the theatre quarter, inherited byte-identical from hylas.journey.json, and is not an attested address.
stops.campa: One dancer, masked, takes every part. A singer or a chorus carries the text, pipes and the beaten scabellum keep the time, and the dancer changes person by changing shape: Agamemnon, then Clytemnestra, then the herald, without a word and without leaving the floor. The mask has no working mouth, so the hands speak, and Roman audiences learn to read hands the way other audiences read faces. This is the instrument Pylades either finds or builds, depending on which ancient sentence is trusted.
suggested_refs: E. J. Jory, 'The Literary Evidence for the Beginnings of Imperial Pantomime', BICS 28 (1981)
Ismene Lada-Richards, Silent Eloquence (2007)
sources: Modern scholarship on imperial pantomime, cited at second hand and flagged as such

stops.name: Rome, three dances taken apart
stops.date_confidence: Attested, undated. Athenaeus, Deipnosophistae 1.20e, citing Aristonicus, credits Bathyllus together with Pylades, who wrote a treatise on dancing, with developing the Italian style out of the comic kordax, the tragic emmeleia and the satyric sikinnis. Athenaeus supplies no year whatever. The date here is borrowed from Jerome's separate entry for the chorus reform and is a placement, not a claim that the two notices report one event. Canonical Rome pin.
stops.campa: The kordax belonged to comedy and was thought indecent. The emmeleia belonged to tragedy and was thought grave. The sikinnis belonged to the satyr play and was thought fast. All three are two centuries out of fashion when Aristonicus reports that Pylades and Bathyllus of Alexandria break them up and build one dance out of the pieces, and that Rome calls the result Italian. Athenaeus keeps the sentence and gives no year for it. He notes in the same breath which of the two men wrote the book about what they had done.
stops.quote: Aristonicus says that this Bathyllus, together with Pylades, who wrote a treatise on dancing, developed the Italian style of dance out of the comic fling called the cordax, the tragic measures called emmeleia, and the satyr rout called sicinnis.
stops.quote_source: Athenaeus, Deipnosophistae 1.20e, citing Aristonicus, tr. C. B. Gulick, Loeb Classical Library
suggested_refs: Athenaeus, Deipnosophistae 1.20e, citing Aristonicus, on the making of the Italian dance
sources: Athenaeus, Deipnosophistae 1.20e, fetched at penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Athenaeus/1B*.html

stops.name: Rome, the chorus sings and the dancer does not
stops.date_confidence: Attested and precisely dated, the one firm date in his whole record. Jerome's Latin continuation of the Chronicle of Eusebius enters under Olympiad 189.3, Abr. 1995 = 22 BCE, that Pylades of Cilicia was the first to have a chorus and a piper perform for him, where previously the performers had sung and danced for themselves. The entry names Pylades alone and does not mention Bathyllus. It does not say the dancer performed silently; it says the chorus and the piper performed for him. Text verified at attalus.org by bathyllus_of_alexandria.journey.json, not refetched this session.
stops.campa: Twenty-two years before the era, in the third year of the hundred and eighty-ninth Olympiad, a chronicle records one change and puts one name on it. Before this, Jerome says, the performers sang and danced for themselves. Pylades of Cilicia is the first to have a chorus and a piper perform for him. It is a division of labour rather than a vow of silence: the body is relieved of carrying the words so that it can carry everything else. Jerome names no source for the notice, dates it to the year and not the season, and gives nothing else about the man in the entry or anywhere near it.
stops.quote: Pylades of Cilicia, a performer of mimes, was the first to have a chorus and piper to perform for him, when his predecessor had sung and danced for themselves.
stops.quote_source: Jerome, Chronicle, Olympiad 189.3 (22 BCE), Abr. 1995, tr. via attalus.org
suggested_refs: Jerome's Latin continuation of the Chronicle of Eusebius, entry for Olympiad 189.3
sources: Jerome, Chronicle, Ol. 189.3, verified at attalus.org/translate/jerome2.html via bathyllus_of_alexandria.journey.json

stops.name: Rome, the book about dancing
stops.date_confidence: Attested that it existed, and nothing beyond that. Athenaeus 1.20e calls Pylades the one who wrote a treatise on dancing. No title, no fragment, no quotation, no manuscript and no named later reader survives; the language it was written in is unknown, as are the place and year of composition. A recurring modern error transfers the treatise to Bathyllus. Date arbitrary. Canonical Rome pin.
stops.campa: He writes a book. Athenaeus, four generations later, knows it existed and mentions it in a subordinate clause, the way one mentions a thing everybody has. Nothing of it survives: no title anybody reports, no sentence anybody quotes, no reader anybody names. A dancer whose art left no notation and no libretto is also the one performer of that generation who set the art down in prose, and the prose went the way of the librettos. What it argued, and whether it was technical or polemical, in Greek or in Latin, nobody records.
suggested_refs: Peri orcheseos, the lost treatise on dancing attributed to Pylades by Athenaeus
sources: Athenaeus, Deipnosophistae 1.20e, fetched at penelope.uchicago.edu

stops.name: Theatre of Pompey, the solemn one
stops.date_confidence: Attested as a characterisation, undated and unlocated. Athenaeus 1.20e sets the two dancers side by side: Pylades solemn, expressing passion and variety of character; Bathyllus jollier, and the composer of a kind of hyporcheme. Athenaeus names no venue and no occasion. The same page contradicts itself, since at 1.20d, on Seleucus's authority, it is Bathyllus who first brings in tragic dancing in the Memphite manner; the contradiction is left standing. Theatre of Pompey pin inherited byte-identical from hylas.journey.json; a working coordinate some three hundred metres west was set aside in favour of the atlas pin.
stops.campa: Pompey's theatre is the only permanent stone house in Rome until Marcellus's is finished, and whatever reaches a general Roman public in these years most likely reaches it here. Athenaeus divides the two men in one line: Pylades solemn, carrying passion and the changes of character; Bathyllus jollier, maker of something like a hyporcheme. The Greek word used of Pylades is polyprosopos, many-charactered, and it describes the range of parts one masked body can take rather than the size of a company.
stops.quote: Pylades' dancing was solemn, expressing passion and variety of character, whereas Bathyllus' was more jolly.
stops.quote_source: Athenaeus, Deipnosophistae 1.37 (Casaubon 20e), tr. C. B. Gulick, Loeb Classical Library
suggested_refs: The Theatre of Pompey, Rome's only permanent stone theatre before 13 BCE
The disputed Memphite clause at Athenaeus 1.20d

stops.name: Rome, a favourite of Maecenas
stops.date_confidence: Attested about the rival, not about him. Cassius Dio 54.17.5 identifies Bathyllus as a fellow artist and a favourite of Maecenas, and Tacitus, Annals 1.54, says independently that Augustus indulged the entertainment to humour Maecenas's passion for Bathyllus. No ancient source names any patron for Pylades. The symmetrical picture in modern accounts, Pylades to Augustus as Bathyllus to Maecenas, is in neither text. Date arbitrary. Canonical Rome pin.
stops.campa: Bathyllus has a house behind him. Dio names it while reporting the quarrel: a fellow artist, and a favourite of Maecenas. Tacitus, writing separately about why the emperor tolerated the whole business, says Augustus was humouring Maecenas's passion for Bathyllus. Behind Pylades the record puts nobody. He is called a dancer and left at that, and the first thing any source shows Augustus doing to him is throwing him out of Italy. Modern accounts supply the missing half anyway, Pylades to Augustus as Bathyllus to Maecenas, and neither Dio nor Tacitus puts a patron behind Pylades.
suggested_refs: Cassius Dio, Roman History 54.17.5, on Bathyllus and Maecenas
Tacitus, Annals 1.54

stops.name: Rome, the freedman he may not have been
stops.date_confidence: Gap. Reference works routinely call Pylades a freedman of Augustus. No manumission record, no Roman tria nomina, no inscription and no ancient text supports it for the Augustan dancer, and the tradition may be a back-formation from the later imperial freedmen who bore the stage name. Recorded here as unattested rather than denied. Date arbitrary. Canonical Rome pin.
stops.campa: The books say freedman of Augustus. There is no stone that says it, no three-part Roman name, no manumission notice, no household record, and no ancient writer who mentions his legal condition in any direction at all. Later centuries do produce real imperial freedmen called Pylades, with proper names and inscriptions of their own, and the status may have walked backward from them onto the founder. Whether the man who made the Italian dance was slave, freed or free while he made it is not in the evidence.
suggested_refs: The absence of any documentary evidence for Pylades's legal status
sources: Assessed as a gap across Suetonius, Cassius Dio, Athenaeus, Macrobius, Jerome and the Suda

stops.name: Rome, far from himself in comedy
stops.date_confidence: Attested, undated, unlocated. Seneca the Elder, Controversiae 3, praefatio 10, uses the two dancers as a figure for specialisation: Pylades in comedy and Bathyllus in tragedy wander far from themselves. The Latin is verified at thelatinlibrary.com by bathyllus_of_alexandria.journey.json. Seneca names no performance, no venue and no year, and the passage is a rhetorician's analogy rather than a review. Date arbitrary. Canonical Rome pin.
stops.campa: A teacher of rhetoric wants an example of a man working outside his own gift and reaches for the two most famous bodies in the city. Pylades in comedy, Bathyllus in tragedy: each of them, Seneca says, wanders far from himself. The line only works on an audience that has watched both attempts and seen both come off badly. So the solemn one does take the light register sometimes, in front of Romans who remember it. Which piece, in what year, before whom, Seneca has no reason to say.
stops.quote: Pylades in comoedia, Bathyllus in tragoedia multum a se aberrant.
stops.quote_source: Seneca the Elder, Controversiae 3, praefatio 10 (Latin, thelatinlibrary.com)
suggested_refs: Seneca the Elder, Controversiae 3, praefatio, on specialisation among performers
sources: Seneca the Elder, Controversiae 3 pref. 10, Latin verified at thelatinlibrary.com via bathyllus_of_alexandria.journey.json

stops.name: Rome, the benches take sides
stops.date_confidence: Attested that the rivalry became public faction, undated. Cassius Dio 54.17.4-5 reports the exile for stasis, sedition, and the rebuke over the quarrel with Bathyllus in one passage, which is the ancient basis for reading the two schools as organised followings; Dio gives no account of what the partisans actually did. Tacitus, Annals 1.54 and 1.77, shows the same factionalism killing people thirty years later. Date arbitrary. Canonical Rome pin.
stops.campa: Rome already divides itself over chariot colours and over gladiators. Now it divides over two men who do not speak. Partisans of Pylades and partisans of Bathyllus fill the same benches, watch the same arm rise, and disagree about what it meant, and the disagreement is organised enough that Dio reaches for the word stasis when he comes to explain the exile. Thirty years later, with both dancers gone from the record, the same factions will kill members of the public, several soldiers and a centurion in one riot.
suggested_refs: Tacitus, Annals 1.54 and 1.77, on the theatrical factions of 14 and 15 CE
sources: Cassius Dio, Roman History 54.17.4-5, fetched at penelope.uchicago.edu
Tacitus, Annals 1.54 and 1.77, cited at second hand from the dossier and from bathyllus_of_alexandria.journey.json

stops.name: Rome, exiled on account of sedition
stops.date_confidence: Attested, and the exile itself is undated. Cassius Dio, Roman History 54.17.4, says only that Augustus restored a dancer called Pylades who had been exiled on account of sedition; the banishment therefore precedes the restoration, and how long it precedes it Dio does not say. Whether Dio's stasis exile and the expulsion Suetonius reports over a pointed finger are one episode or two cannot be settled from the texts, and neither is used to date the other. Date arbitrary. Canonical Rome pin.
stops.campa: The record does not show him being sent away. It shows him being brought back, and mentions in passing what he had been sent away for. Stasis, faction, the word a Greek historian uses for a city turning on itself. Dio does not say what was done, by whom, in which year, or whether Pylades did any of it himself rather than being the thing people did it about. Was he an agent of the disorder or its occasion? The one sentence that records the expulsion is a subordinate clause inside a sentence about the recall, and it does not say.
suggested_refs: Cassius Dio, Roman History 54.17.4, the only notice of the exile for stasis
sources: Cassius Dio, Roman History 54.17.4, fetched at penelope.uchicago.edu

stops.name: Rome, restored
stops.date_confidence: Attested and dated to 18 BCE by position in Dio's annalistic narrative. Cassius Dio 54.17.4 records the restoration among measures that reconciled the public to the strictness of Augustus's other regulations; Dio 54.18.1 opens the following year with the consulship of Gaius Furnius and Gaius Silanus, consuls of 17 BCE, so chapter 17 belongs to 18 BCE. An earlier working note attaching the passage to 13 BCE, on a misreading that put Crassus and Lentulus here, was wrong and is withdrawn. Dio names no site for the return.
stops.campa: Augustus brings him back. Dio files the recall among the concessions that made the rest of the regime's discipline bearable, next to a relaxation of what the praetors were allowed to spend on their festivals: the emperor tightening the law on marriage and public conduct with one hand and returning the city's favourite dancer with the other. How long the exile lasted, where the order reached him, and whether he came back to the same theatre, Dio does not say. He says that afterwards people stopped remembering the strictness.
stops.quote: Thus, even if some were vexed at the strictness of his other regulations, yet by reason of this action and also because he restored one Pylades, a dancer, who had been exiled on account of sedition, they remembered them no longer.
stops.quote_source: Cassius Dio, Roman History 54.17.4, tr. Earnest Cary, Loeb Classical Library
suggested_refs: Cassius Dio, Roman History 54.17, and the consular headings that date it to 18 BCE
sources: Cassius Dio, Roman History 54.17.4 and 54.18.1, fetched at penelope.uchicago.edu

stops.name: Palatine, it is to your advantage, Caesar
stops.date_confidence: Attested, undated, unlocated. Cassius Dio 54.17.5 has Augustus rebuke Pylades for quarrelling with Bathyllus, a fellow artist and a favourite of Maecenas, and Pylades reply with the sentence quoted. Dio writes in the early third century CE and no verbatim value attaches to reported speech at that distance. He names no setting and does not date the exchange relative to the recall; the Palatine pin, Augustus's residence, is inherited byte-identical from hylas.journey.json and is a plausible but unattested placement.
stops.campa: The emperor reproaches him for feuding with a colleague. Pylades answers by telling the princeps what the dancers are for: it is to your advantage, Caesar, that the people should devote their spare time to us. It is not an apology and it is not a defence of the art. It is an argument from public order, offered to the man who has spent twenty years converting a republic's attention into his own, by an entertainer who has worked out that he is part of the machinery. Dio reports no answer from Augustus.
stops.quote: It is to your advantage, Caesar, that the people should devote their spare time to us.
stops.quote_source: Pylades to Augustus, Cassius Dio, Roman History 54.17.5, tr. Earnest Cary, Loeb Classical Library
suggested_refs: Cassius Dio, Roman History 54.17.5, the quarrel and the reply
sources: Cassius Dio, Roman History 54.17.5, fetched at penelope.uchicago.edu

stops.name: Rome, Campus Martius: he takes a pupil
stops.date_confidence: Attested as a fact, undated. Macrobius, Saturnalia 2.7.12, writing in the early fifth century CE, says only that Pylades was famous in his art in the time of Augustus and brought his pupil Hylas up by instruction to a contest of equality. No school, address or teaching site is named anywhere; the Campus Martius pin marks the theatre quarter and is not attested. hylas.journey.json places the same scene at 20 BCE; both placements are arbitrary and the source gives no year.
stops.campa: He takes a pupil and teaches him everything. The training of a pantomime is training in silence: the dancer never speaks, the chorus carries the words, and every meaning the audience will get has to arrive through an arm or the tilt of a masked face. Macrobius, four centuries later, puts the whole apprenticeship into one clause: Pylades brought Hylas on by instruction as far as a contest of equality. He records no school, no address, no other pupil, and not one word from Pylades about the arrangement.
stops.quote: Hylam discipulum usque ad aequalitatis contentionem eruditione provexit.
stops.quote_source: Macrobius, Saturnalia 2.7.12
suggested_refs: Macrobius, Saturnalia 2.7.12-19, the only connected ancient account of the teaching
sources: Macrobius, Saturnalia 2.7.12, Latin at penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/L/Roman/Texts/Macrobius/Saturnalia/2*.html

stops.name: Rome, the people divide
stops.date_confidence: Attested, undated. Macrobius, Saturnalia 2.7.13, states the division of popular favour in one sentence and gives no year, no venue, and no account of what the partisans did. Date arbitrary and orders the segment. Canonical Rome pin, inherited byte-identical from virgil.journey.json.
stops.campa: The pupil comes level and the city splits. Macrobius gives it one sentence: the people were then divided between the votes of the two. Pylades has invented the form, and half the benches now prefer a man he trained. There is no record of what he said about it in private, because there is no record of him in private at all. What survives is what he did in public, which was to begin correcting his own pupil out loud, in front of the paying house, in Greek.
stops.quote: Populus deinde inter utriusque suffragia divisus est.
stops.quote_source: Macrobius, Saturnalia 2.7.13

stops.name: Theatre of Pompey, the shout from the benches
stops.date_confidence: Attested, undated, unlocated. Macrobius, Saturnalia 2.7.13: Hylas dances a piece ending on the words the great Agamemnon and measures out something lofty and huge; Pylades calls the correction across the theatre in Greek. Macrobius names no theatre and no year. Theatre of Pompey pin inherited byte-identical from hylas.journey.json, which stages the same occasion from the pupil's side.
stops.campa: He has come to watch, and he does not wait for the piece to end. Hylas, dancing to a line that closes on the great Agamemnon, shows greatness by showing size: an arm sweeping out the height and the breadth of a king. Two senses of one Greek word, and the pupil has taken the wrong one. From the benches, in Greek, over the heads of a house that is following half of it by ear, the master calls the correction across the whole theatre: you are making him tall, not great.
stops.quote: Σὺ μακρὸν οὐ μέγαν ποιεῖς
stops.quote_source: Pylades to Hylas, Macrobius, Saturnalia 2.7.13
suggested_refs: Macrobius, Saturnalia 2.7.13-14, the Agamemnon exchange entire
sources: Macrobius, Saturnalia 2.7.13, Latin and Greek at penelope.uchicago.edu

stops.name: Theatre of Pompey, the crowd makes him dance it
stops.date_confidence: Attested in Macrobius, Saturnalia 2.7.14, as the continuation of the same occasion; undated, and the venue is unnamed in the source. The date is a sequencing device and not a claim of a second day. Same pin and same caveat as the previous stop.
stops.campa: The audience will not let the criticism stand as words. They force him onto the floor to dance the same piece himself, and at the line he had faulted he measures nothing at all. He shows Agamemnon thinking. Nothing, he holds, suits a great commander better than to think on behalf of everybody. Within the hour the same benches have watched two definitions of one Greek word danced against each other. It is the one surviving account of what Pylades's own body did on a stage, and what it did was stop moving. Macrobius reports no verdict from the crowd.
stops.quote: Tunc eum populus coegit idem saltare canticum cumque ad locum venisset quem reprehenderat, expressit cogitantem, nihil magis ratus magno duci convenire quam pro omnibus cogitare.
stops.quote_source: Macrobius, Saturnalia 2.7.14
suggested_refs: Macrobius, Saturnalia 2.7.14
sources: Macrobius, Saturnalia 2.7.14, Latin at penelope.uchicago.edu

stops.name: Theatre of Marcellus, two words at the Oedipus
stops.date_confidence: Attested in Macrobius, Saturnalia 2.7.15, undated. Macrobius says Pylades rebuked the dancer's securitas, his unconcern, with the cry Su blepeis, you are looking. He never mentions blindness, never says which episode was danced, and never names a venue; the blind-Oedipus reading is a modern completion, plausible and unattested. Theatre of Marcellus pin inherited byte-identical from hylas.journey.json, where it stands in for a second Augustan theatre and is not evidenced. Earlier working notes gave the correction as 'You are using your eyes'; the Greek is two words and is rendered here literally.
stops.campa: Hylas dances Oedipus and the master corrects him again, this time in two words. You are looking. Macrobius says the target was the dancer's securitas, the ease of a body moving as though nothing in the world were hidden from it. Later readers supply the obvious completion, that a blinded man should not move like a man who can see, and Macrobius supplies nothing of the kind. The entire surviving technical estate of the founder of Roman pantomime is this: two corrections, five Greek words, both shouted at somebody else.
stops.quote: Saltabat Hylas Oedipodem, et Pylades hac voce securitatem saltantis castigavit: Σὺ βλέπεις.
stops.quote_source: Macrobius, Saturnalia 2.7.15

stops.name: Theatre of Pompey, arrows into the benches
stops.date_confidence: Attested in Macrobius, Saturnalia 2.7.16, undated and unlocated. Macrobius says that when he danced the mad Hercules and seemed to several people not to keep the bearing proper to a performer, incessum histrioni convenientem non servare, he pulled off his mask and rebuked the ones who were laughing. Earlier working notes described the complaint as one of excess and had Augustus reproving him for it; both are wrong and the correction is recorded here. Venue and date are the atlas's placement, not the source's.
stops.campa: He is dancing the madness of Hercules and he shoots at the audience. Macrobius does not say whether the arrows are real or the bow is mimed; what he specifies is the objection, which is that the man on the floor was not carrying himself the way a performer carries himself. Pylades pulls the mask off his own face, the one thing the art forbids, and shouts at the ones who were laughing: fools, I am dancing a madman. He has stopped performing in order to explain that he was performing. Whether he put the mask back on and finished the piece, Macrobius does not report.
stops.quote: Μωροί, μαινόμενον ὀρχοῦμαι.
stops.quote_source: Pylades to the laughing spectators, Macrobius, Saturnalia 2.7.16

stops.name: Palatine, the same piece in the dining room
stops.date_confidence: Attested in Macrobius, Saturnalia 2.7.17, undated and unlocated. Macrobius says that when he performed the same role in the triclinium at Augustus's order he drew the bow and let the arrows fly there too, and that Caesar was not annoyed at having been put by Pylades in the same position as the Roman people. Macrobius names no house; the Palatine pin, Augustus's residence, is inherited byte-identical from hylas.journey.json and is a plausible but unattested placement. Earlier notes made this a private request following an imperial reproof; the text has an order and no reproof.
stops.campa: Augustus orders the piece repeated indoors. Pylades dances the madman in the dining room, and in the dining room he draws the bow again and lets the arrows go among the couches. Macrobius records the emperor's reaction in one clause of Latin: Caesar was not annoyed at having been put by Pylades in the same position as the Roman people. The man who has just been shot at over his own dinner takes the point as a remark about the art. Nothing at all is said about the other guests.
stops.quote: Nec indignatus est Caesar eodem se loco Pyladi quo populum Romanum fuisse.
stops.quote_source: Macrobius, Saturnalia 2.7.17

stops.name: Palatine, answering the emperor in Homer
stops.date_confidence: Attested in Macrobius, Saturnalia 2.7.18, undated and unlocated. Asked by Augustus what he had contributed to dancing, Pylades answered with a line of Homer, Iliad 10.13. Macrobius reports no question about an older and simpler manner, and no explanation about the scale of Roman spectacle; the answer is a bare quotation, and reading it as a claim about the chorus and pipes built around the solo dancer is inference, though Jerome's 22 BCE entry independently attests that reform. Palatine pin as in the previous stop.
stops.campa: Augustus asks him what he has contributed to the art of dancing. He does not answer in his own words. He gives a line out of the Iliad, from the passage where Agamemnon looks toward the Trojan plain at night and hears what is coming off it: the sound of pipes and reed flutes, and the din of men. The dancer who never speaks on stage answers the emperor in Greek hexameter and adds nothing to it. Macrobius records no follow-up question, offers no gloss of his own, and does not say how the line was taken.
stops.quote: Αὐλῶν συρίγγων τ' ἐνοπὴν ὁμαδόν τ' ἀνθρώπων
stops.quote_source: Pylades to Augustus, quoting Homer, Iliad 10.13, in Macrobius, Saturnalia 2.7.18

stops.name: Circus Flaminius, the quarrel leaves the theatre
stops.date_confidence: Attested that a populi seditio arose from the contention held between Pylades and Hylas: Macrobius, Saturnalia 2.7.19. Undated, and no site is given; the date is arbitrary. The pin marks the Circus Flaminius at the southern end of the Campus Martius, an area of public assembly beside the theatres, inherited byte-identical from hylas.journey.json, and is not an attested location for any disturbance.
stops.campa: The argument about how to dance Agamemnon becomes an argument in the streets. Macrobius calls it a populi seditio, a rising of the people, and traces it straight to the contention held between master and pupil. It is the same word Dio uses for the ground of the exile, in a different author writing four centuries later about a different rival. Whether Rome rioted over Pylades once or twice, and whether the two accounts are two reports of a single week, the record does not decide.

stops.name: Palatine, you are ungrateful, king
stops.date_confidence: Attested in Macrobius, Saturnalia 2.7.19: Augustus's roused indignation over the riot, and Pylades's reply. Undated; the date orders the segment. Macrobius names no setting, and the Palatine pin is inherited byte-identical from hylas.journey.json. The reply is close in sense to the one Dio gives at 54.17.5 but the words differ and the rival differs, and the two must be quoted apart rather than merged.
stops.campa: The riot reaches the emperor and the emperor's anger falls on him. He answers in Greek and does not apologise: you are ungrateful, king; let them busy themselves about us. It is the second time in the record that he tells a princeps that public absorption in dancers is a service rendered to the state, and the second time he does it in the imperative. Macrobius records no reprisal in the sentence. Suetonius, in another book and without saying the incidents are connected, records that Augustus had Hylas flogged and Pylades put out of Italy.
stops.quote: Καὶ ἀχαριστεῖς, βασιλεῦ· ἔασον αὐτοὺς περὶ ἡμᾶς ἀσχολεῖσθαι.
stops.quote_source: Pylades to Augustus, Macrobius, Saturnalia 2.7.19

stops.name: Theatre of Pompey, the spectator who hissed
stops.date_confidence: Attested, undated and unlocated. Suetonius, Divus Augustus 45.4, fetched at penelope.uchicago.edu, gives the cause of the expulsion as the pointed finger and the redirected crowd, and names no theatre, no year and no spectator. Theatre of Pompey pin inherited byte-identical from hylas.journey.json and is the atlas's placement, not the source's; note that the Theatre of Marcellus was already in partial use by 17 BCE, so the inference from Rome having one stone theatre holds cleanly only for the earlier window.
stops.campa: One man in the benches is hissing. Pylades, on the floor, raises his arm and points at him, and the whole house turns and looks where the arm is aiming. It takes a second, and it is the exact skill he has spent his life building, the arm that makes a theatre see what is not in front of it, used once on a real man sitting in a real seat. Suetonius reports it in a single clause among the punishments Augustus handed out to performers. What became of the spectator is not recorded.
stops.quote: Pylades was expelled from the city and from Italy as well, because by pointing at him with his finger he turned all eyes upon a spectator who was hissing him.
stops.quote_source: Suetonius, Divus Augustus 45, tr. J. C. Rolfe, Loeb Classical Library (1913), via LacusCurtius

stops.name: Rome, put out of Italy
stops.date_confidence: Attested as to the sentence, blank as to the destination. Suetonius, Divus Augustus 45.4, says Augustus removed him from the city and from Italy as well. No source names where he went, how long he was away, who went with him, or how he lived; the road out is a genuine gap and no coordinates are invented for it. The pin marks Rome, the place he is expelled from. Whether this is Dio's stasis exile under another description is unresolved. Date arbitrary. Canonical Rome pin.
stops.campa: The sentence is not banishment from the city. It is banishment from the city and from Italy as well, which is the difference between removing a man from an audience and removing him from a trade. Where he goes, nobody writes down. Not Cilicia, not Greece, not anywhere: the record skips the years entirely. He is a professional whose profession exists in one city, and the emperor has taken the city away from him. Suetonius gives the sentence in one clause and moves straight on to the next performer on his list.

stops.name: Rome, the two rivals the tradition merges
stops.date_confidence: A source conflict, stated and not resolved. Cassius Dio 54.17.4-5 puts Bathyllus opposite Pylades in the quarrel that draws the emperor's rebuke and sits in the narrative for 18 BCE. Macrobius, Saturnalia 2.7.19, gives the same shape of episode with the pupil Hylas in Bathyllus's place, different Greek in Pylades's mouth, and no year at all. Neither account is used here to fill the other's gaps, and the merged version that circulates in modern retellings, including an exile of Hylas, is reported by no ancient writer. Date arbitrary. Canonical Rome pin.
stops.campa: Two authors, two centuries apart, give him the same scene with a different opponent. In Dio the rival is Bathyllus and the reply is about the people's spare time. In Macrobius the rival is his own pupil and the reply calls the emperor ungrateful. Modern retellings weld the two together and produce an exile of Hylas that no ancient writer reports. Bathyllus keeps the version in Dio and Hylas keeps the version in Macrobius. Which rival was standing there when he said it, or whether he said it twice, is not something the two texts can be made to settle.
suggested_refs: The unresolved relation between Cassius Dio 54.17.4-5 and Macrobius, Saturnalia 2.7.19
sources: Cassius Dio, Roman History 54.17.4-5
Macrobius, Saturnalia 2.7.19

stops.name: Theatre of Marcellus, a second and a third stone house
stops.date_confidence: Attested as to the buildings, unattested as to him. The Theatre of Balbus was dedicated in 13 BCE; the Theatre of Marcellus was completed in 13 and formally inaugurated in 12, with ancient notices varying between 13 and 11, and part of the ludi saeculares had already been held in it in 17 BCE. An earlier working note had both theatres dedicated by Augustus in 13 BCE, which is wrong. No source places Pylades in either building. Pin inherited byte-identical from hylas.journey.json. The date marks the buildings, not an event in his life.
stops.campa: For thirty-five years Rome has had one permanent stone theatre. Now it has three. Balbus dedicates his in 13; Marcellus's is finished in the same year and opened by Augustus in 12, though it had already taken part of the secular games five years before that. The art Pylades assembled out of three dead Greek dances has the room for it now, three times over, in the middle of the capital. No source puts him in any of the three. He is alive, and that is all these years establish.
suggested_refs: The Theatre of Balbus, dedicated 13 BCE, and the Theatre of Marcellus, inaugurated 12 BCE

stops.name: Forum of Augustus, the old man in the insignia
stops.date_confidence: Attested by Cassius Dio, Roman History 55.10.11, and firmly dated to 2 BCE by position: the notice stands between the appointment of the first two praetorian prefects, Quintus Ostorius Scapula and Publius Salvius Aper, and the disgrace and banishment of Julia. Dio names no venue; the Forum of Augustus and the Temple of Mars Ultor were dedicated in the same year, so the placement is chronologically apt and otherwise unsupported. An earlier working note treated this as a late secondary tradition with no primary basis; it is Dio, and it is primary.
stops.campa: Twenty years after the exile he gives a festival. Dio records that he performed none of the work himself, being very old, but wore the insignia of office and paid the cost of the entertainment. That is a magistrate's posture, taken by a dancer. The man who was put out of Italy for pointing at a spectator now stands in the ceremonial dress of the men who fund public games, in the year Augustus dedicates his own forum. Dio does not say what was danced at these games, or by whom, or where.
stops.quote: Pylades, the dancer, gave a festival, though he did not perform any of the work himself, since he was very old, but merely wore the insignia of office and provided the cost of the entertainment.
stops.quote_source: Cassius Dio, Roman History 55.10.11, tr. Earnest Cary, Loeb Classical Library

stops.name: Rome, knights and women of rank on the stage
stops.date_confidence: Attested by Cassius Dio, Roman History 55.10.11, in the same passage as the festival and dated with it to 2 BCE. Dio reports that on this occasion knights and women of rank were brought onto the stage, and pairs the notice with a festival given by the praetor Quintus Crispinus. Dio does not say at which of the two festivals the highborn performers appeared, and names none of them. Canonical Rome pin, inherited byte-identical from virgil.journey.json.
stops.campa: Dio adds one line to the notice of the festival and does not explain it. On this occasion knights and women of rank were brought onto the stage. Roman law and Roman shame both keep the equestrian order and the daughters of good houses on the far side of the floor from performers, and here they are on the wrong side of it, at games funded by a Cilician dancer wearing the insignia of office. Dio pairs the entry with a festival given by the praetor Quintus Crispinus and leaves it there.

stops.name: Rome, no death, no tomb, no will
stops.date_confidence: A gap, confirmed rather than asserted. No ancient source records the date, place, cause or circumstances of Pylades's death, nor any retirement, last performance, illness, testament, heir, funeral or grave. The absence was checked across every witness available for this file: Suetonius, Cassius Dio, Athenaeus, Macrobius, Jerome, Seneca the Elder and the Suda. The date closes the traceable record at the last notice that certainly concerns him and is not a death date.
stops.campa: The record stops with an old man in ceremonial dress paying for a show. There is no death year, no city, no cause, no grave, no epitaph, no will, no heir, and no ancient writer who thought any of that worth a line. He is not recorded dying under Augustus, who outlives the last notice of him by sixteen years, and he is not recorded living either. For the man who made the form that filled the theatres of the empire for four hundred years, the evidence ends inside a sentence about somebody else's praetorship.
suggested_refs: The absence of any death notice, tomb or testament for Pylades of Cilicia
sources: Assessed as a gap across Suetonius, Cassius Dio, Athenaeus, Macrobius, Jerome and the Suda

stops.name: Tibur, his name on a rival's stone
stops.date_confidence: Attested, undated, findspot disputed. CIL VI 10115 = ILS 5197 records the pantomime Theoros boasting of victories over four named dancers, the first of them Pylades of Cilicia. Modern scholarship places the stone in the late first century BCE or the first century CE; the date here is arbitrary and opens the segment, and hylas.journey.json places the same stone at 10 BCE. The CIL VI number assigns it to Rome while the Theatrum lexicon calls it a grave inscription from Tibur, and the conflict is unresolved; the pin is inherited byte-identical from hylas.journey.json. Whether its Pylades is this one cannot be proved.
stops.campa: The only stone anywhere with his name on it was paid for by a man who beat him. Theoros, a pantomime, lists his defeated: Pylades of Cilicia, Nomius of Syria, Pierus of Tibur, Hylas of Salmacis. Four names, four countries, one boast. It is the nearest thing to a professional register the art produced, and it survives because a winner wanted his own name kept beside better ones. Where the stone lay before it was catalogued is disputed, Rome by its number and Tibur by the lexicon that describes it.
stops.quote: Pylades aus Kilikien, Nomius aus Syrien, Pierus aus Tibur und Hylas aus Salamakis
stops.quote_source: Theatrum lexicon, entry on Theoros, summarizing CIL VI 10115 = ILS 5197

stops.name: Rome, stat per successores
stops.date_confidence: Attested in the Latin. Seneca the Younger, Naturales Quaestiones 7.32.3, composed in the early to mid 60s CE, verified at thelatinlibrary.com by bathyllus_of_alexandria.journey.json. Domus can mean house, lineage or school and Seneca does not disambiguate. The passage documents institutional succession under the two names some eighty years after the quarrel; the date is the approximate composition date, not an event. Canonical Rome pin.
stops.campa: Seneca complains that the philosophical schools have died out while nobody lets a pantomime's name drop, and then says the thing that turns out to be the whole afterlife: the house of Pylades and Bathyllus stands through successors, these arts have many pupils and many teachers, and all over the city the private stage is sounding. Eighty years after the rivalry the two enemies are one noun. Whether domus here means a building, a bloodline or a technique handed on, the Latin will not decide.
stops.quote: Stat per successores Pyladis et Bathylli domus, harum artium multi discipuli sunt multique doctores; priuatum urbe tota sonat pulpitum.
stops.quote_source: Seneca the Younger, Naturales Quaestiones 7.32.3 (Latin, thelatinlibrary.com)

stops.name: Puteoli, other men of the name
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction, and flagged as unverified. The stage name Pylades recurs among later imperial pantomimes, including a performer active under Trajan and the wealthy imperial freedman Lucius Aurelius Pylades honoured at Puteoli in the later second century CE. Neither the Trajanic notice nor the Puteoli inscription was independently verified for this file; both are carried from the research dossier and should be checked against an epigraphic database before use. The date is approximate. Puteoli pin inherited byte-identical from bathyllus_of_alexandria.journey.json.
stops.campa: The name goes on working after him. Later dancers take it, including one active under Trajan and an imperial freedman, Lucius Aurelius Pylades, whom Puteoli honours in the second century with a full Roman name and a stone. He has the two things the founder never had in the record: a legal identity and a monument of his own. Reference works have been folding the men together for centuries. Neither the Trajanic notice nor the Puteoli stone has been checked against an epigraphic database, and both stand as leads rather than attestations.

stops.name: Constantinople, the entry that keeps the village
stops.date_confidence: Attested as a text, garbled as history. Suda pi 3159 gives the Cilician origin, the village of Mestarne, and the invention of the Italic dance from the kordax, the sikinnis and the emmeleia. The entry drops Bathyllus and swaps sikinnis and emmeleia against Athenaeus and the standard account; the Suda On Line editors call it a confused version of Athenaeus 1.20e. A separate entry, Suda omicron 671, credits Augustus with inventing pantomime and names Pylades and Bacchylides, a corruption of Bathyllos, as its first practitioners. Neither entry mentions the chorus and pipes, a reform earlier notes wrongly assigned to the Suda. The tenth-century compilation date is approximate; pin inherited byte-identical from egeria.journey.json.
stops.campa: A thousand years later a Byzantine compilation copies out a sentence about him and gets most of it wrong. It hands the invention of the Italian dance to Pylades alone, drops Bathyllus entirely, and reverses which old dance belonged to tragedy and which to the satyr play. Its own modern editors call the entry a confused version of Athenaeus. And in the middle of the confusion sits the one detail no other text preserves, that he came from a village called Mestarne. The garbled entry is the only reason anyone knows he came from anywhere smaller than a province.
stops.quote: A Cilician, from the village of Mestarne. He wrote about Italic dance, which was also invented by him, from the so-called comic dance which was called the kordax; and [from] the tragic, which was called sikinnis; and [from] the satyric, which [was called] emmeleia.
stops.quote_source: Suda, s.v. Pylades (pi 3159), Suda On Line translation
suggested_refs: Suda pi 3159 and Suda omicron 671, the two Byzantine notices

stops.name: Lyon, a medallion under a museum label
stops.date_confidence: Attested as an object and a label, unresolved as an identification. A Roman terracotta medallion was shown at the Musee Lugdunum, Lyon, in the exhibition SPECTACULAIRE! Le divertissement chez les Romains, photographed on 4 December 2022 and catalogued on Wikimedia Commons as a medallion bearing the likeness of the pantomime Pylade. A holding institution given in earlier notes as the Musee Ziem, Martigues, could not be confirmed and is dropped. Nothing establishes that the object depicts the Augustan founder rather than a later performer of the name, and no securely identified ancient portrait of him is known.
stops.campa: There is one object in the world that carries his name on a label. A small Roman terracotta medallion, shown at Lyon in 2022 in an exhibition about how Romans amused themselves, catalogued as bearing the likeness of the pantomime Pylade. Which Pylades the label does not say and cannot say, since the name was worn by dancers for centuries after the Cilician. No secure ancient portrait of him exists. The images that circulate under the name mostly show Orestes's companion, the silent friend out of the tragedies.
